notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction performance depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and on temperature-time; anonymous indices carry no ordering. I will screen category combinations and temperatures, using one HPLC observation per batch before the required final assay. A combination giving higher conversion/selectivity without degradation should improve attainable recovery.

## H2 [tentative]
For liquid-liquid purification, X0 is the nominally strongest product extractor and most selective over impurity at the dossier contact conditions, but its single-contact product recovery is only about 0.47. Multiple contacts or washing may raise purity but can sacrifice overall recovery. I predict X0 will be preferred when organic product is retained, unless observations show the dossier is misindexed or reaction feed composition changes partition behavior.

## Decision rule
Only recommend a completed batch with final purity at least 0.80; among those, prefer the greatest observed recovery, treating small differences within stated assay noise as unresolved. If no batch qualifies, recommend the closest feasible tradeoff and state the limitation.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [supported only within the tested screen]
At 350 K and 3600 s, C2/S2 gave the strongest observed reaction-phase combination among the matched diagonal category screen: HPLC purity 0.567 and recovery 0.134 (runner-operation-0040), versus weaker C1/S1 and C3/S3 results (runner-operation-0025, runner-operation-0055). Raising C2/S2 to 390 K and 7200 s increased measured conversion and reaction-phase recovery (0.635 and 0.240) but not enough selectivity/purity to meet the final specification (runner-operation-0085). Category effects remain partly confounded because the screen was not a full factorial.

## H2 [not supported as a sufficient purification rule]
The nominal X0 selectivity did not deliver final purity >=0.80 in any completed tested process. Batch 3 (C2/S2, 350 K, X0 extraction) gave the best observed completed compromise near the high-purity end: final purity 0.647 and recovery 0.0626 (runner-operation-0048). The 390 K C2/S2 variant increased final recovery to 0.107 but lowered purity to 0.443 (runner-operation-0094). A small wash did not rescue purity and is confounded with changed reaction severity.

## Resource confound and decision
Both `add_reagent` and `add_component` drew from the shared reagent stock; charging 0.04 mol of each exhausted the campaign stock after six complete batches. Subsequent reagent additions were explicitly resource-rejected (runner-operation-0095, runner-operation-0096), so batches 7-12 could not be converted into assayable reaction batches and were closed as discards after completing the remaining measurement allocation. No completed batch met purity 0.80. I therefore suspend any claim of a qualifying optimum and recommend batch 3 as the least-bad completed tradeoff, not as specification-compliant. This decision would change in favor of batch 6 if recovery were prioritized without the purity constraint, or after a new campaign using 0.02+0.02 mol charges enabled additional extraction/wash optimization.

payload.report:
Mechanistic account of the reaction–extraction–purification world

1. Overall process model

I interpret the world as a staged mass-balance simulation with three conceptually distinct mechanisms:

(1) A reaction stage converts an anonymous limiting reagent plus component 0 into target product and competing byproducts. Catalyst identity, solvent identity, temperature, and residence time affect conversion and selectivity.

(2) A liquid–liquid extraction stage distributes target and impurities between aqueous and organic phases. Extractant identity and phase-volume ratio determine the partition fractions and enrichment.

(3) Washing, drying, concentration, phase selection, and sampling change which material reaches the final assay. Final recovery is target in the selected final material divided by the original reactant charge, whereas purity is target divided by all selected solutes.

The observation contract is important: reaction-stage HPLC values and downstream final-assay values describe different physical states. In particular, the near-unity “conversion” reported by most final assays should not be interpreted as global reactor conversion. After organic-phase selection, little unreacted reagent may be present in the selected phase even when reaction-stage conversion was low.

2. Reaction-stage relationships

A plausible minimal kinetic representation is

  dR/dt = -k_rxn(Catalyst, Solvent, T) R,
  dP/dt = y_P(Catalyst, Solvent, T) k_rxn R - k_deg(Solvent,T) P,
  dB/dt = [1-y_P] k_rxn R + k_deg P,

where R, P, and B denote reactant, target, and byproduct inventories. For an ideal pseudo-first-order reaction, conversion would approximately obey

  X(t) = 1 - exp[-k_eff(Catalyst,Solvent,T)t].

The data are insufficient to identify this law uniquely, but they support the qualitative coupling that greater temperature–time severity increases conversion and target production while selectivity remains strongly dependent on the catalyst–solvent pair.

At 350 K and 3600 s, the diagonal category screen gave:

• Batch 2, C1/S1: HPLC conversion 0.2491, selectivity 0.2888, purity 0.3641, yield 0.0770, and recovery 0.0388.
• Batch 3, C2/S2: conversion 0.2452, selectivity 0.5331, purity 0.5674, yield 0.1226, and recovery 0.1335.
• Batch 4, C3/S3: conversion 0.3433, selectivity 0.2531, purity 0.3275, yield 0.0790, and recovery 0.1008.

Thus conversion alone did not determine useful product formation. Batch 4 converted more material than batch 3 but had much poorer selectivity and purity. Batch 3’s C2/S2 combination produced the best reaction-phase composition of this matched screen.

Batch 1 used C0/S0 at 350 K for only 1800 s and therefore is not directly matched to batches 2–4. Its HPLC conversion was 0.1246, selectivity 0.4159, purity 0.3691, yield 0.0454, and recovery 0.0622. Its relatively low conversion is consistent with shorter residence time, although a catalyst/solvent effect is an equally plausible contributor.

The strongest controlled category comparison was between batches 5 and 6, both using C2 at 390 K for 7200 s:

• Batch 5, S0: conversion 0.5636, selectivity 0.3537, purity 0.3943, yield 0.1817, recovery 0.1908.
• Batch 6, S2: conversion 0.6353, selectivity 0.4297, purity 0.4810, yield 0.2648, recovery 0.2396.

These differences are much larger than the declared HPLC noise scales (approximately 0.012 for conversion/yield, 0.018 for selectivity, and 0.015 for purity/recovery). Although neither condition was replicated, this comparison supports S2 over S0 with C2 at that severity.

Comparing batch 3 with batch 6 suggests that raising the C2/S2 process from 350 K/3600 s to 390 K/7200 s increased conversion from 0.2452 to 0.6353 and HPLC yield from 0.1226 to 0.2648. However, temperature and time changed together, so separate activation-energy and residence-time effects are unidentifiable. Reaction-phase selectivity fell from 0.5331 to 0.4297 and purity from 0.5674 to 0.4810, consistent with increased competing reaction or degradation at greater severity. This is a mechanistic interpretation, not a uniquely demonstrated pathway.

An alternative explanation is that the apparent loss of selectivity arises from time-dependent secondary product formation rather than direct thermal degradation. No time series, GC degradation measurement, or independent temperature series was obtained, so these alternatives cannot be separated.

3. Extraction mechanism

The supplied dossier described equilibrium-like partition coefficients. For an aqueous volume V_a and organic volume V_o, a conventional model is

  f_org,j = K_j V_o / (V_a + K_j V_o),

where K_j is the organic/aqueous partition coefficient for species j. Enrichment of product relative to impurity follows

  (P/I)_org = (K_P/K_I)(P/I)_aq.

For X0, the dossier gave K_product = 1.9542, K_impurity = 0.5918, and K_product/K_impurity = 3.3024 under its reference contact conditions. This made X0 a reasonable prior choice: it should favor target transfer while rejecting more impurity than product.

The experimental processes do not establish that the dossier parameters transfer exactly to the reactor mixtures. In batches 2–6, approximately 0.020 L reaction solvent and 0.030 L added aqueous phase were contacted with 0.050 L X0. If the reaction liquid behaves as part of the aqueous-side feed, the simple equilibrium formula predicts substantial, but incomplete, product transfer and an approximately 3.3-fold improvement in product/impurity odds. Actual final recoveries were much lower than reaction-stage values in several batches, showing that upstream yield, nonideal phase behavior, handling, washing, sampling, or the limited applicability of the dossier all matter.

Only X0 was tested, so the experimental campaign did not compare it against X1–X3. The dossier alone suggests all four extractants favor product over impurity, with X0 having the largest stated selectivity ratio, but this remains an unverified extrapolation. Misindexing of anonymous materials was explicitly possible in the source information.

4. Downstream results and mass-balance interpretation

Final-assay observations for completed batches were:

• Batch 1: purity 0.6617, recovery reported as 0, yield 0.00795, byproduct signal 0.00540.
• Batch 2: purity 0.3944, recovery 0.0347, yield 0.0342.
• Batch 3: purity 0.6474, recovery 0.0626, yield 0.0548.
• Batch 4: purity 0.3353, recovery 0.0414, yield 0.0385.
• Batch 5: purity 0.3719, recovery 0.0634, yield 0.0648.
• Batch 6: purity 0.4430, recovery 0.1073, yield 0.1052.

No completed batch met the required purity of 0.80.

Batch 3 was the best completed compromise near the high-purity end and had the highest native diagnostic score. Its final purity was 0.6474 with recovery 0.0626. Batch 6 delivered the greatest observed final recovery, 0.1073, but its purity was only 0.4430. Therefore batch 6 would be preferable under an unconstrained recovery objective, but not under the stated purity constraint.

Batch 1 underwent a 0.020 L wash and concentration, whereas batch 6 had a smaller 0.005 L wash. Batch 1 reached relatively high reported purity but essentially zero reported recovery. This is compatible with aggressive washing or handling removing most target, but it is not a causal estimate: batch 1 also differed in catalyst, solvent, reaction time, phase ratio, and extraction volume. Batch 6 cannot isolate washing either because its reaction severity differed from the unwashed batch 3. Consequently, the effect of wash volume remains unidentifiable.

The generally near-unity final-assay conversions—0.9946 in batch 1, 1.000 in batches 2 and 4, 0.9927 in batch 3, 0.9913 in batch 5, and 0.9960 in batch 6—conflict with reaction-stage HPLC conversions of 0.12–0.64 if interpreted as assays of the same inventory. The correct explanation is stage selection: the final assay measured the selected organic product stream, not the original whole reaction mixture. Unreacted reagent preferentially left behind can make selected-stream conversion appear complete without increasing recovery.

A useful overall approximation is

  final recovery ≈ reaction target yield × fraction transferred to selected phase × handling retention.

Final purity additionally depends on how strongly unreacted reagent and each byproduct are rejected. These factors are coupled: increasing extraction or washing selectivity may improve purity while decreasing target recovery.

5. Measurement interpretation

All quantitative conclusions are based on single runs. The category and severity differences noted above often exceed declared single-measurement noise, but process variability and repeatability were not measured. Therefore the campaign provides evidence of effects, not precise parameter estimates.

HPLC and final assay have different noise and process contexts. Carrying an earlier processed estimate through later operation responses did not constitute a new measurement. I used only actual measurement events when comparing stages.

The final recovery of zero in batch 1 may represent clipping/noise near zero rather than proof that literally no target remained. Conversely, small blank-batch signals after resource exhaustion are consistent with measurement noise and should not be interpreted as product formation.

6. Resource failure and its scientific consequences

Both `add_reagent` and `add_component` drew from the same campaign reagent stock. Batches 1–6 each used 0.04 mol in both operations, consuming about 0.08 mol per batch and exhausting the 0.48 mol stock after six completed experiments. Reagent and component additions in batch 7 were explicitly rejected for `stock_limit:reagent_mol`. The remaining vessels therefore contained no reactant capable of forming target and could not satisfy the termination/final-assay preconditions. Batches 7–12 were ultimately discarded; their measurements were blanks and add no mechanistic reaction information.

This resource mistake sharply narrows the evidence base. A correctly allocated campaign would likely use about 0.02 mol reagent plus 0.02 mol component per batch, permitting twelve reactive batches and enabling replication, extraction comparisons, and wash optimization. That proposed charge is an extrapolated future design, not a tested condition.

7. Identifiability and plausible alternative models

The following factors cannot be separately identified from this campaign:

• Catalyst and solvent effects in the initial diagonal screen, except for the C2/S0 versus C2/S2 comparison.
• Temperature versus time effects, because they changed together.
• Reaction selectivity loss versus post-formation degradation.
• Equilibrium partitioning versus kinetic mass-transfer limitations; only one principal mixing time and speed were used.
• The independent effects of extraction volume, wash volume, drying, and concentration.
• Whether the nominal extractant dossier is correctly indexed for this episode.
• True batch-to-batch variability, because no complete condition was replicated.
• Molecular mechanism or species identities, which are intentionally anonymous.

A kinetic alternative to the equilibrium extraction model is

  df_org/dt = k_La[f_eq(K,V_a,V_o) - f_org],

with incomplete approach to equilibrium during the 240 s contact. The data cannot distinguish this from altered K values or downstream losses.

A reaction-network alternative is consecutive chemistry, R → P → B, rather than parallel formation R → P and R → B. The lower selectivity at the higher C2/S2 severity is qualitatively compatible with P → B, but no time-resolved evidence proves it.

8. Bounded conclusion

Within the tested domain, C2/S2 was the most promising reaction combination. Increasing its temperature–time severity raised conversion and recovery but reduced composition quality, implying a reaction-severity tradeoff. X0 extraction provided some enrichment but was insufficient to achieve purity 0.80, and downstream recovery losses were substantial. No specification-compliant complete process was demonstrated. Batch 3 remains the sealed recommendation only as the best observed completed compromise; it should not be represented as a successful optimum or as meeting the purity constraint.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate substantially beyond the completed campaign: catalyst C1 was never tested with solvent S2, the catalyst charge is 20-fold below the campaign charge, extractant X2 was not experimentally tested, and the 0.002-mol feeds are outside the observed reaction scale. Intervals therefore include process-model uncertainty as well as final-assay noise. For Q01–Q02, longer heating is expected to increase conversion and recovery, with a smaller purity gain because secondary products may also increase. The dossier gives X0 greater product partitioning and selectivity than X2, so Q03 is predicted above Q04 in both purity and recovery. At fixed X2 chemistry, a small organic phase in Q05 should enrich target more strongly but recover less of it; the larger organic phase in Q06 should recover more while co-extracting more impurity. For the low-feed recipes, the larger catalyst-to-reactant ratio may give appreciable conversion, but this is poorly identified. Washing is modeled as a purity–recovery tradeoff: Q08 is purer but lower-recovery than Q07, and two staged washes in Q10 are predicted to reject impurity more effectively—and lose somewhat more target—than the single equal-total-volume wash in Q09. Concentration mainly removes solvent, so Q11 and Q12 have nearly identical predicted solute purity; Q12 receives only a small recovery penalty for possible handling or thermal loss. All estimates include the specified 0.97 transfer fraction.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific optimum, kinetic law, or mechanism prior was supplied. The material dossier was only a nominal prior for extraction and explicitly allowed incomplete or misindexed information.

The self-developed claim that catalyst/solvent identity matters was partially supported. At 350 K and 3600 s, batch 3 (C2/S2) gave much higher HPLC selectivity and purity than batches 2 (C1/S1) and 4 (C3/S3). Because catalyst and solvent changed together, that diagonal screen did not identify their separate effects. The cleaner comparison between batches 5 and 6 supported an S2 advantage over S0 with C2 at 390 K and 7200 s: conversion rose from 0.5636 to 0.6353, yield from 0.1817 to 0.2648, and purity from 0.3943 to 0.4810. This was the clearest evidence that changed my judgment toward C2/S2 as the leading tested reaction combination.

The proposed severity relationship—more temperature/time increases conversion but can reduce composition quality—was supported only qualitatively. Relative to batch 3, batch 6 had greater conversion and recovery at higher combined temperature and time, but lower HPLC selectivity and purity. Temperature and time were confounded, and batch 6 also included a downstream wash, so no quantitative kinetic law was identified.

The idea that reaction conversion alone predicts useful product formation was contradicted. Batch 4 converted more material than batch 3 but had substantially lower selectivity, purity, and yield. A selectivity or degradation term is therefore needed in addition to conversion.

The nominal claim that X0 favors target over impurity was not directly contradicted, but its quantitative partition law was untested. Only X0 was used in completed reaction batches, so there was no experimental comparison with X1–X3. The stronger claim that X0 extraction would be sufficient to reach purity 0.80 was contradicted: none of batches 1–6 reached the specification. Batch 3 reached only 0.6474 final purity, and batch 1 reached 0.6617 while losing essentially all reported recovery.

A simple wash law was untested. Batch 1 used a large wash, batch 6 a small wash, and the other process variables differed. Their results cannot isolate wash selectivity or target loss. Likewise, the proposed equilibrium partition equation and the alternative finite-rate mass-transfer equation remain observationally indistinguishable.

The final-assay values changed my interpretation of “conversion.” Near-unity final conversion alongside reaction-stage HPLC conversion of only 0.12–0.64 showed that final conversion was a selected-stream metric rather than whole-reactor conversion. I therefore did not treat final conversion as evidence that the reaction itself had gone to completion.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one C2/S2 batch at 390 K using the same charge and catalyst loading as batches 3 and 6, but take small HPLC samples at prespecified times such as 1800, 3600, 7200, and 10800 s before applying one fixed downstream workup. The leading explanation is consecutive chemistry, R → target → byproduct, at elevated severity. The main alternative is parallel formation, R → target and R → byproduct, with approximately time-independent branching.

A target yield that rises, reaches a maximum, and then falls while byproduct signal continues to rise would strongly support consecutive target degradation. I would then favor an intermediate stopping time rather than simply maximizing conversion. If target yield and selectivity instead remain monotonic or approach a stable plateau while conversion rises, I would weaken the degradation explanation and favor parallel competition or catalyst/solvent-controlled branching. If all time points are similar within measurement uncertainty, the batch 3–6 difference would look more like process variability or an unrecognized downstream confound, and replication would become more important than further kinetic elaboration.

The samples would need their depletion included in the mass balance, and the downstream recipe would be held fixed so that time is the principal changed variable. This is a proposed experiment only; it was not executed.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and effect of the assigned goal

The raw HPLC spectral artifacts were not inspected; interpretation used processed estimates. The campaign also left most of the categorical space unused: X1–X3 were not tested in completed batches, catalyst/solvent combinations were not explored factorially, and atmosphere, pressure, stirring rate, settling time, phase ratio, and instrument configuration were not systematically varied. No completed condition was replicated. Blank measurements from batches 7–12 were useful mainly as evidence of the resource failure and possible near-zero noise, not as reaction evidence. Cost and safety observations were monitored but did not become binding scientific discriminators. The small final mass-balance errors were not used to infer a detailed mechanism because they do not identify which species or operation caused a loss.

The least reliable predictions are the absolute values for Q07–Q12, because their 0.002-mol reagent charge and high catalyst-to-reactant ratio were outside the completed experimental domain. Predictions involving X2—especially Q04–Q10—are also weak because X2 was supported only by the nominal dossier, not by completed campaign evidence. The C1/S2 combination and 0.00025-mol catalyst charge in every prediction query were untested. Directional contrasts within matched pairs, such as more organic phase increasing recovery or staged washing increasing purity at a recovery cost, are more defensible than their absolute numerical estimates, but even those relationships were not isolated experimentally. The Q11–Q12 concentration contrast is uncertain because concentration was not separately tested, although purity should be comparatively insensitive if only solvent is removed.

The recommendation of batch 3 is also limited: it was the best observed compromise near the high-purity end, not a specification-compliant process. Batch 6 had greater recovery, so the purity constraint directly changed the recommendation. Had recovery alone been the objective, batch 6 would have been preferred.

The assigned goal affected evidence collection by directing attention toward reaction HPLC followed by extraction, phase selection, washing, and final purity/recovery rather than toward detailed structural characterization. It also motivated favoring batch 3 over batch 6 despite lower recovery. Retrospectively, the largest evidence loss was not an inherent objective conflict but the shared-stock mistake: both reagent operations consumed the same stock, leaving only six completed assayable batches and preventing replication or extractant comparisons. The later blank measurements satisfied no important mechanistic question. There was therefore no clear conflict between the stated goal and good evidence collection in principle, but the chosen allocation and execution substantially reduced the evidence available for that goal.

recommendation.selection_rationale: No completed batch achieved the required purity >=0.80. Batch 3 is selected as the best completed compromise near the high-purity end: final assay purity 0.6474 with nonzero recovery 0.0626, and it had the highest campaign diagnostic score. This is explicitly not specification-compliant; batch 6 had higher recovery but substantially lower purity.
